n: In this lecture we study section 1.2: opium, omnopon, morphine, narcotine, codeine, meconic acid and meconin, and the methods of isolating and analysing them. Key terms: opium, omnopon, meconic acid, meconin, morphinism, the Marquis, Fröhde and Wagner reagents, Rf and morpholate. The outline is as follows: opium and omnopon, meconic acid and meconin, morphine, codeine, and finally narcotine.

First let us clarify the difference between opiates and opioids. Opiates are similar in structure to morphine and are ND obtained from it: morphine, codeine, heroin, that is diacetylmorphine, and the main metabolite 6-monoacetylmorphine. Opioids act like morphine but belong to another chemical group: promedol, methadone, fentanyl and others. This group of alkaloids of narcological significance consists chiefly of the opium alkaloids, whose molecule contains an isoquinoline nucleus.

Classification of opium alkaloids. Isoquinoline derivatives are divided into two subgroups: phenanthrene-isoquinoline derivatives and benzylisoquinoline derivatives. The phenanthrene series includes morphine, codeine and thebaine. The benzyl series includes papaverine and narcotine. That is, which subgroup an alkaloid belongs to depends on its structure.

How opium is obtained and what properties it has. Opium, that is the black drug, is obtained from the juice of the unripe fruit of the poppy. The skin of the capsule is incised, and the juice that oozes out is scraped off when it dries in the air. Ibn Sina, in the Canon of Medicine, called the black drug afyun. The product is a dark brown thick residue or powder with a characteristic smell and a bitter taste. It is partly soluble in water, and its aqueous solution is acidic.

Composition of opium. Opium contains more than 60 alkaloids, with a total content of up to 15-20%. According to the literature, morphine is 19%, narcotine 8-10% and codeine 1.5-3%, and thebaine and papaverine are also present. The alkaloids occur as salts with meconic acid, so meconic acid is also determined. Opium may contain protein substances, carbohydrates, salts, organic acids and meconin.

Use of opium and proof of its presence. In medicine, opium powder, extract, alcoholic solution and tablets have been used. All drugs based on opium have a narcotic action and cause morphinism. Opium is absorbed into the blood through the gastrointestinal tract or parenterally; when smoked, it enters the blood directly through the lungs. The finding of morphine, codeine, narcotine and meconic acid proves the presence of opium in the sample.

Omnopon, that is pantopon, is a mixture of the hydrochloride salts of opium alkaloids: 50% morphine and 32-35% other alkaloids. It is a reddish-yellow powder, soluble in water at 1:15 and in ethyl alcohol at 1:50, and its aqueous solution foams strongly when shaken. The 1% solution in an ampoule contains 6.7 mg of morphine, 2.7 mg of narcotine, 0.72 mg of codeine, 0.36 mg of papaverine and 0.05 mg of thebaine. An important difference: omnopon contains no meconic acid or meconin. If morphine, codeine and narcotine are found and meconic acid is not, omnopon was taken.

Properties of meconic acid. Meconic acid occurs in opium combined with the alkaloids. On prolonged boiling it breaks down to CO2 and comenic acid, then to β-hydroxypyrone. It is poorly soluble in cold water, ethyl alcohol and diethyl ether, and readily soluble in hot water and boiling ethyl alcohol. It is extracted from an acid medium with organic solvents. Remember: if morphine, codeine, narcotine or other opium alkaloids are found, the examination for meconic acid is always carried out as well.

The procedure for isolating meconic acid. The biological specimen is acidified with hydrochloric acid, steeped with ethyl alcohol and filtered. The filtrate is evaporated to dryness. The residue is dissolved in water and boiled, MgO is added, and the mixture is filtered hot. The filtrate is evaporated to a small volume, hydrochloric acid is added, and it is tested for meconic acid.

Identifying meconic acid. With iron(III) chloride a blood-red colour forms, and the colour does not change on heating. In the UV spectrum an aqueous solution of meconic acid gives maxima at 210, 284 and 303 nm. The method is also used to isolate meconic acid from food residues, urine and vomit. The sensitivity of the reaction is low and meconic acid breaks down quickly in a biological specimen, so the sample is analysed promptly. If 0.05 g of opium was taken, it may be detected.

About meconin. Meconin occurs in opium poppy and in some plants. In the pure state it is a white powder melting at 102°C, and forms salts in alkali solutions. It is poorly soluble in cold water and readily soluble in hot water, ethyl alcohol, diethyl ether, benzene and chloroform, and is extracted from an acid medium by organic solvents. Narcotine or hydrastine are converted into meconin under the action of weak reducing agents. It is not used in medicine and has no narcological significance, but its detection confirms the use of opium.

Isolating and identifying meconin. The minced specimen is steeped with ethyl alcohol, acidified with sulphuric acid, filtered, evaporated and extracted with benzene. The benzene layer is separated and evaporated, and the residue is tested for meconin. When concentrated sulphuric acid is added to the residue, a green colour forms, which turns red if kept for two days. On slow heating, a green-emerald colour forms, then pink, and finally red again.

Now morphine. Morphine is the principal alkaloid of opium; it was isolated from poppy fruit in 1806, and its chemical structure was established in 1925. Because of its hypnotic action it was named morphine after Morpheus, the god of sleep. As the base it is a fine crystalline powder of rhombic shape, with a melting point of 253-254°C. It is poorly soluble in cold water, relatively well soluble in boiling water, and poorly soluble in ether, benzene and chloroform. Its aqueous solution is alkaline, and with alkalis it forms a morpholate.

Morphine salts and losses. In medicine the acetate, hydrochloride, sulphate and tartrate salts are used. All the salts are practically insoluble in diethyl ether and chloroform. Morphine combines rapidly with protein substances, forming complex conjugates. These compounds do not pass completely into the liquid layer in the acidified alcohol or water methods. As a result, the main part of the morphine is lost.

The narcological significance of morphine. In medicine morphine is used chiefly as the hydrochloride and is considered the main representative of the narcotic analgesics. It relieves pain strongly, lowers the sensitivity of the pain centres of the brain, and is used to relieve shock in severe injuries. The pain centres are paralysed and sleep comes on, and the sensitivity of the respiratory and cough centres is reduced. Morphine and all agents containing it cause morphinism. If morphine is found in physical evidence, morphine, opium or omnopon may have been taken.

Morphinism and routes of administration. Morphinism includes opium and its preparations, that is pantopon, omnopon, paregoric, laudanon, pectol and opionon, as well as morphine, codeine, thebaine, heroin, phenadone and promedol. Habituation to morphine-type drugs develops relatively quickly. Opium is taken by mouth, or injected under the skin or into a vein. The powder is snorted or smoked. Codeine is taken by mouth, and morphine and promedol are injected. Injection with unsterilised syringes causes the transmission of various infectious diseases.

Morphine poisoning: autopsy and distribution. In poisoning with morphine or its preparations, pathological-anatomical examination gives no characteristic signs. In opium poisoning, an odour of opium sometimes comes from the stomach, and there may be brown residues and haemorrhages in the brain and heart. About 30% of morphine goes to the liver, kidneys and lungs, and in the liver it loses its toxic properties. The minimum lethal dose is 0.1-0.5 g, sometimes 0.06 g.

Acute morphine poisoning. Because of tolerance, drug addicts can take 10 times the normal dose or more. In acute poisoning, euphoria, dry mouth, tinnitus, headache, sweating, and disturbance of heart and respiratory rhythm are seen. In severe cases there are cyanosis and paralysis of the respiratory centre. Euphoria is replaced after 30-40 minutes by drowsiness. The withdrawal syndrome begins several hours after the last dose and lasts 5-7 days.

Opium preparations and doses. The smallest amount of morphine that kills a person is about 0.1-0.5 g, sometimes 0.06 g. Children are very sensitive to morphine: 1-2 drops of tincture of opium kill a young infant. The preparations taken by drug addicts fall into groups. Opiates: opium, meconic acid, morphine. Semisynthetic opiates: heroin, codeine, hydromorphone. Synthetic opiates: meperidine, propoxyphene, methadone. Mixed opiates: pentazocine, butorphanol, buprenorphine.

Table 1 lists the opiate preparations taken by drug addicts. The opiates include opium, that is a mixture of alkaloids, and meconic acid, and also morphine. Semisynthetic opiates: heroin, codeine, hydromorphone. Synthetic opiates: meperidine, propoxyphene, that is Darvon, and methadone. Mixed opiates: pentazocine, that is Talwin, butorphanol and buprenorphine. The narcotic analgesics include morphine, omnopon, promedol and fentanyl.

Metabolism of morphine. Morphine forms a glucuronide with glucuronic acid: 50% in the first 8 hours, and after 24 hours about 90% is excreted in the urine as the glucuronide. In part it is N-demethylated to normorphine and O-methylated to codeine. In cadaver organs it changes gradually, forming pseudomorphine and dihydromorphine. On prolonged standing in the open air, or by oxidation in the body, it forms oxymorphine, which is more toxic and stable. It cannot be reduced back to morphine.

t: Isolating opium alkaloids from blood and urine
n: Isolating opium alkaloids from blood and urine. Sodium bisulphate is added to blood or urine, which is heated for 30 minutes in a boiling bath, and after cooling trichloroacetic acid is added. The protein precipitate is filtered off, and the filtrate is brought to pH 6.5-7.0 with 25% ammonia. Then NaHCO3 is added and the mixture is extracted twice with butanol-chloroform 1:9, and the extract is passed through anhydrous Na2SO4. Two portions result: one for TLC and one for reactions.

Identifying morphine by TLC. The residue is dissolved in 0.5 ml of butanol-chloroform 1:9 and applied to the starting line of the plate. As markers, solutions of morphine, codeine and heroin are applied. The system is ethyl acetate-methanol-25% ammonia in the ratio 17:2:1. When the front has risen 10 cm, the plate is dried and Marquis or Fröhde reagent is applied. The detection limit for morphine is 10-15 µg. From blood up to 83% can be isolated and identified, and from urine up to 71%.

Table 2 gives Rf and spot colours. The sorbent is silica gel, and the system is ethyl acetate-methanol-25% ammonia 17:2:1. Morphine has Rf 0.32-0.39, and its spot is red-pink with Marquis and pink with Fröhde. Codeine: Rf 0.39-0.52. Dionine: Rf 0.41-0.46. Heroin: Rf 0.52-0.66. Narcotine Rf=0.66-0.75, papaverine Rf=0.79-0.83. Narcotine gives a pink colour with Marquis and a blue-green colour with Fröhde.

Colour reactions of morphine. With Marquis, Fröhde, Mandelin and Erdmann reagents, morphine and other opium alkaloids form a violet colour. Iron(III) chloride gives a bluish-green colour with the phenolic hydroxyl of morphine. The sensitivity is low, but the reaction is important in distinguishing morphine from other opium alkaloids. Codeine, heroin and dionine do not react with iron(III) chloride, because the hydrogen of the phenolic hydroxyl has been replaced by radicals. With a mixture of potassium hexacyanoferrate(III) and iron(III) chloride, a blue solution or precipitate forms.

t: Morphine: Wagner reagent and pharmacological test
n: Wagner reagent and the pharmacological test. Wagner reagent, that is iodine in KI, gives a crystalline precipitate with morphine: rectangular plates. The sensitivity is 0.03 mg of morphine. Atropine, brucine, caffeine, scopolamine and other alkaloids do not form microcrystals of this shape. In the pharmacological test, morphine instilled into the eye of laboratory animals constricts the pupil.

Identifying morphine in the second TLC system and by UV spectrum. System 2 is ether-acetone-25% ammonia in the ratio 40:20:2. Dragendorff reagent modified by Mune is used, Rf=0.18, and the spot is reddish brown. In the UV spectrum the base gives a maximum at 287 nm in ethanol, at 250 and 296 nm in 0.1 M NaOH, and at 284 nm in 0.1 M H2SO4. An aqueous solution of morphine hydrochloride and sulphate absorbs maximally at 285 nm.

IR spectrum of morphine and its quantification. In the IR spectrum, a KBr disc absorbs in the regions of 805, 1243, 1448 and 945 cm-1. The quantity is determined by the spectrophotometric method from the UV spectra. In the photocolorimetric method with the silicomolybdate complex, silicic acid, HCl, ammonium molybdate and ammonia are used, a blue colour forms, and 0.2-4 mg of morphine can be determined. The quantity is also determined by GC-MS or HPLC-MS.

Identifying morphine by microcrystalloscopy. On a microscope slide, the dry residue is dissolved in a drop of 0.1 M HCl, the reagent is applied, and after 10-15 minutes it is examined under the microscope. With a 15% solution of cadmium iodide, a white precipitate forms, then a cluster of needle-shaped crystals, with a detection limit of 2.5 µg of morphine. With Reinecke salt solution, a cluster of pink needle-shaped crystals forms, with a detection limit of 2 µg of morphine.

Now codeine. Codeine is the monomethyl ether of morphine, identified in 1832; the codeine used in medicine is synthesised from morphine. It is a strong base, a colourless bitter crystalline powder, readily soluble in water, diethyl ether, alcohol and chloroform, with a melting point of 153-155°C. It is insoluble in alkali solutions, and this distinguishes it from morphine. In an alkaline medium, at pH=8-9.5, it is extracted by organic solvents better than morphine.

Narcological significance and metabolism of codeine. Codeine is widely used in medicine, and habituation is possible. It does not completely paralyse the sensory nerve endings, does not constrict the pupil, and stops cough. In large amounts it poisons, and signs similar to morphine poisoning are seen. The maximum single dose is 0.05 g. It is metabolised in three directions: to the glucuronide; by O-demethylation to morphine; and by N-demethylation to norcodeine, which is excreted as the glucuronide. A very small part is excreted unchanged.

Reactions for detecting codeine. With Dragendorff, Mayer and other precipitating reagents it gives a characteristic coloured precipitate. With Marquis reagent, that is formaldehyde and concentrated H2SO4, a pale violet colour forms, with a sensitivity of 0.05 mg of codeine. With Fröhde reagent, that is a solution of ammonium molybdate in concentrated H2SO4, a dirty blue and then a bluish-green colour forms. This is highly characteristic of codeine, with a sensitivity of 0.1 µg. A mixture of iron(III) chloride and K3[Fe(CN)6] gives no colour, because codeine has no free phenolic group.

Codeine: TLC, UV and IR. In TLC the system chloroform-acetone-diethylamine 50:30:2 is used. With Dragendorff reagent modified by Mune, a brown-reddish spot is seen at Rf=0.40. In the UV spectrum an alcoholic solution of codeine base gives a maximum at 286 nm. In the IR spectrum a KBr disc absorbs in the regions of 1052, 1268 and 1500 cm-1.

Separating codeine from morphine, and quantifying codeine. The chloroform extract from the alkaline medium is evaporated and alkali is added to the residue. Morphine, as the morpholate, does not pass into ether, whereas codeine passes into the ether layer. Therefore the organic layer is tested for codeine and the aqueous layer for morphine. The quantity of codeine is found by UV spectrophotometric determination of the alcoholic solution. The extraction-photometric method is also used, that is the ion associate with tropaeolin 00, as well as GC-MS and HPLC-MS.

Identifying codeine and dionine by microcrystalloscopy. Codeine gives a yellow amorphous precipitate with a saturated solution of picrolonic acid, then yellow spheroids and white-yellow plates appear, with a detection limit of 1 µg. Codeine with a 5% solution of mercury(II) chloride and rubbing with glass gives needle-shaped and plate-shaped crystals, with a detection limit of 13 µg. Dionine gives a cluster of needle-shaped and prismatic crystals, with a detection limit of 14 µg.

The last alkaloid is narcotine. Narcotine is an opium alkaloid and a weak base, poorly soluble in water and readily soluble in organic solvents. In the pure state it is not used in medicine. Its detection in a biological specimen indicates abuse of opium or omnopon. It does not cause addiction, and its action is similar to papaverine, but its toxicity is stronger. In the body it quickly passes from the blood into the tissues, and is excreted in the urine unchanged within 6 hours, and thereafter as conjugates.

t: Identifying narcotine and separating it from morphine
n: Identifying narcotine and separating it from morphine. With concentrated sulphuric acid, first a yellow and then a reddish colour forms, and after a few days a cherry red. In TLC, the system chloroform:acetone:25% ammonia in the ratio 30:30:2 is used, and with Dragendorff reagent modified by Mune a pink-brown spot is seen. When morphine is found, narcotine is also tested for. Because the reaction results are the same, narcotine is separated from morphine: the chloroform residue is dissolved in dilute HCl, made alkaline with NaOH and extracted with chloroform. The quantity is determined by extraction-photometric methods, GC-MS and HPLC-MS.

t: Case: which substances are tested for when morphine is suspected
n: Case solution. Blood was brought to the forensic chemical examination, and the preliminary analysis raised the suspicion of morphine. Step one: identify morphine by colour reaction, TLC, UV and IR. If morphine is found, codeine and narcotine are also tested for. Meconic acid gives a blood-red colour with iron(III) chloride, and meconin is also tested for. The use of opium is proved by the finding of morphine, codeine, narcotine and meconic acid. If all are found, it is opium; if meconic acid is absent, it is omnopon. Distinguishing morphine from codeine is based on iron(III) chloride and on solubility in alkali.

To conclude. The use of opium is proved by the finding of morphine, codeine, narcotine and meconic acid, that is meconin, whereas omnopon contains no meconic acid or meconin. Morphine and codeine are distinguished by the phenolic hydroxyl, that is by iron(III) chloride and by solubility in alkali. For confirmation, TLC, UV, IR and microcrystalloscopy are used. Review questions: what distinguishes opium from omnopon; meconic acid and meconin; what is oxymorphine; how to distinguish morphine from codeine, heroin and dionine; how to isolate from liquid materials.
